NC.scope: city fees and county fees outside municipalities under separate enabling statutes
NC.reason: City council sets stormwater rates after hearing with at least seven-day newspaper notice. Rates may account for impervious surface, use, runoff and other listed factors, and may not exceed service costs. Only one local unit may levy for a joint overlapping program. Farm and airport exemptions/limits require separate handling; County153A-277 separately permits fees outside municipalities with parallel hearing, cost and overlapping-program limits. Bona fide farm uses and military runways/taxiways are exempt; other airport runway/taxiway exemption requires specified reinvestment and certification.

localGrant.description: City160A-314 and county153A-277 authorize fees within their respective service geography, with hearing, cost, overlapping-program and exemption safeguards; county fee area excludes municipalities.
localGrant.changedBy: State legislature amends the enabling statute; municipal council sets or revises charges within it. Local ordinance cannot override state conditions or exemptions.

federalLink.program: Federal Power Act interstate electricity and wholesale market jurisdiction
federalLink.match: Regulatory jurisdiction boundary; not a matching grant or uniform cost share.
conditions: Wholesale means resale under section201(d). Interstate transmission and jurisdictional wholesale rates are federal; retail rates are not ordinarily set by FERC.
Section201(f) excludes listed governmental and cooperative entities from ordinary PartII regulation unless a provision specifically reaches them; exceptions prevent a blanket municipal exemption.

The statute compilation is through2018 amendments;2025 agency guidance corroborates the core boundary. Later amendments, specific preemption cases, ERCOT and territorial exceptions still need consolidation.

verification.promptClaim: 3. **Local taxes for transportation need state permission.** Local-option sales taxes for transportation are allowed in many states but not all. Some need voter approval (California: two-thirds for a special tax, under Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, lowered to 55% for some measures; **verify** current thresholds). Availability belongs on each place's fiscal-authority record (the game has `92N_NATIONAL_STATE_LOCAL_FISCAL_AUTHORITY`).
verification.finding: Proposition 5 would have lowered some local infrastructure bond approvals to 55%; official 2024 results rejected it. Do not apply 55% to transportation special taxes. Citizen-initiative special taxes and school bonds require separate legal classification.

verification.promptClaim: - **State, then local:** revenue sharing of fuel tax and registration fees by formula (the formula is a state setting); state preemption of local speed limits (varies: some states let cities set 20 or 25 mph by ordinance, and Oregon and Washington expanded this, **verify**); state approval of local tolling.
verification.finding: The marked Oregon/Washington expansion claim is verified: Oregon2017 Portland residential grant expanded to all cities2019; current eligible residential reduction up to10mph with20mph floor. Washington20mph nonarterial/10mph shared streets have separate procedures and state-highway approval. Neither is universal county power. Revenue-sharing formulas and toll routes remain separate research work.

verification.promptClaim: 1. **Fuel tax rate, and indexing it to inflation.** State. About 22 states index or vary their rate (**verify** count, ITEP). Effect: gasoline demand elasticity about -0.05 to -0.1 short run, -0.3 long run (Hughes, Knittel and Sperling 2008; Brons and others 2008). Revenue falls about 0.84% a year as fuel economy rises (already in the game). Available in every state and D.C.; territories set their own. Local fuel taxes are allowed in about 12 states (**verify**).
verification.finding: ITEPJuly2025 and NCSLMay2025 report26states+DC but mix current/future designs: COindexingFY2032–33, WAfirst2% adjustmentJuly2026, MSindexingJuly2029 after fixed steps. January2026 active-index count unresolved. HKSshort-run2001–06 range−.077 to−.034; Bronsmeta mean−.34 short/−.84 long, not claimed−.3. Full-text ranges/horizons unverified, so no Brons runtime coefficient admitted.

verification.promptClaim: 1. **Fuel tax rate, and indexing it to inflation.** State. About 22 states index or vary their rate (**verify** count, ITEP). Effect: gasoline demand elasticity about -0.05 to -0.1 short run, -0.3 long run (Hughes, Knittel and Sperling 2008; Brons and others 2008). Revenue falls about 0.84% a year as fuel economy rises (already in the game). Available in every state and D.C.; territories set their own. Local fuel taxes are allowed in about 12 states (**verify**).
verification.finding: Current nationwide local fuel-tax count remains unresearched;2009 count cannot establish2026 law. Gasoline-price elasticity contrast corrected in item1; tax transfer needs retail-price pass-through and tax share, not direct substitution.

verification.promptClaim: 3. **Electric vehicle registration fee.** State. More than 30 states charge one, typically $50 to $200 a year. Effect: a small drop in electric vehicle sales (**verify** study).
verification.finding: Jenn2018 fixed-effects observational model reports0.24% lower EV sales per$1 enacted fee over2010–June2018 data. Implementation coefficient is smaller and statistically nonsignificant. This is study-specific, not universal causation. January2026 fee count remains unresolved. NCSLJuly2026 reports at least42states and35hybrid-fee states but includes future NM2027 and NJ2028 schedule amounts. Primary NM2026 act confirms delayed2027 start; primary NJMVC schedule exceeds$200 already byJan2026. This survey is not an active-Jan2026 count.

verification.promptClaim: 4. **Tolling and congestion pricing.** State law must authorize it, and federal approval is needed on federal-aid highways (the Value Pricing Pilot Program). Example: New York's Manhattan central business district tolling, which started January 5, 2025, at $9 a car at peak. Effect: traffic entering the zone fell about 7 to 11% in the first months (MTA reports, **verify**), with transit ridership up. Available only where state law authorizes it.
verification.finding: MTA reports 11% fewer zone entries over its first six months of 2025. This is an observed program comparison, not a universal causal coefficient. Initial peak car toll was$9 and launchJanuary 5,2025.

verification.promptClaim: 7. **Complete streets and Vision Zero rules.** State and city. More than 1,700 complete-streets policies nationwide (Smart Growth America, **verify**). Effect: pedestrian deaths down where speeds drop; a lower speed limit of 20 mph cuts pedestrian fatality risk sharply (AAA Foundation, Tefft 2011).
verification.finding: SGA2025 report verifies more than1700 adopted policies; older1600 page was stale. Tefft2013 links impact speed to conditional pedestrian death risk, not direct effect of lowering a posted limit. No automatic policy-to-fatality coefficient admitted.

verification.promptClaim: 8. **Automated speed and red-light cameras.** State law authorizes or bans them, and cities deploy them. About 20 states ban or limit speed cameras (IIHS, **verify**). Effect: red-light cameras cut fatal red-light crashes about 21% in large cities (IIHS 2011).
verification.finding: Canonical September2026 IIHS speed rows explicitly list prohibitions inID,ME,MS,NH,NJ,TX,WV,WI; SC generally prohibits with emergency exception. No-law rows are not bans; permitted systems may have narrower site limits. About20 lacks a defined category.2011 fatal red-light study24%,2016 study21%.

verification.promptClaim: - **Special district:** most transit is run by an authority (for example SEPTA, MARTA, King County Metro, which is a county department, and Denver RTD), with board seats appointed by member governments or elected (Denver RTD's board is elected, **verify**).
verification.finding: RTD states it has 15 publicly elected directors. King County Metro is a county department, not evidence that every transit operator is a special district.

verification.promptClaim: - **Member governments:** board appointment shares and a cost-sharing formula; a member may withdraw where state law allows it (Michigan towns opted out of SMART, **verify**).
verification.finding: SMART2020 records historical community opt-in/out. Oakland2022 countywide millage removed former gaps. PA236/2024 enactedJanuary17,2025 effectiveApril2,2025 amends withdrawal124.458;>=1.1m-county exclusion/all-member trigger follows expiration of millage then in force. Existing obligations survive; current universal local opt-out claim is wrong.

verification.promptClaim: 4. **Bus lanes and signal priority.** City. Effect: bus speeds up 5 to 15% (NACTO, **verify**).
verification.finding: NYCDOT reports14thStreet pilot maxima24% speed/30% ridership, which does not verify a generic NACTO5–15% range. Original monitoring tables and comparable counterfactual remain unverified; no universal numerical effect admitted.

verification.promptClaim: 7. **Transit-oriented zoning near stations.** State and city. Example: California SB 79 (2025) allows height near transit (**verify** passage). See Zoning.
verification.finding: SB 79 approvedOctober 10,2025 asChapter 512. Local applicability generally beginsJuly 1,2026; other provisions have different schedules.

verification.promptClaim: **Availability:** local transit taxes are barred where state law doesn't enable them. Some states give no dedicated local option (**verify** list, APTA).
verification.finding: Not yet resolved against dated primary evidence; original figure not adopted.

verification.promptClaim: 1. **Fund or drop a state-supported Amtrak route.** State. It carries an annual appropriation. Examples: Virginia's Transforming Rail in Virginia (2019 to 2021, bought rail right of way, **verify**); Indiana funded, then ended, the Hoosier State (2019).
verification.finding: Virginia2020 authority law and2021 CSX acquisition verified. INDOT identifies funding loss and final Hoosier State runJune30,2019; federally supported Cardinal is a separate service.

verification.promptClaim: - Effect: route ridership. Virginia's routes grew strongly after frequency was added (**verify** figures). Road trips shift, and emissions fall per diverted trip.
verification.finding: VPRA management discussion reports FY2024 ridership1,384,665 and FY2025 ridership1,451,276. This section is unaudited. The increase alone does not identify frequency effects; a harmonized2015–2025 corridor panel remains unresolved.

verification.promptClaim: - Availability: every state may fund it. Old "internal improvements" clauses once barred state railroad investment (Michigan 1850, Wisconsin 1848). Wisconsin later amended its constitution to allow transportation appropriations (**verify** the year and article), and Michigan funds its routes through its transportation fund. **Research: each state's current constitutional credit, gift and internal-improvement clauses as they apply to rail.**
verification.finding: Wisconsin ArticleVIII§10(2)(e) rail appropriation exception and§7(2)(a)1 debt authority were addedApril1992; highway exception1908 and ports1960 are separate. Proposed general transportation amendment was rejected1975 and1976. Historical primary text resolves year/article; live official consolidation and nationwide clause matrix remain gaps.

verification.promptClaim: 2. **Create and fund a high-speed or new intercity rail authority and bond.** State. Example: California Proposition 1A (2008). Effect: capital spending and jobs; ridership only when a segment opens. Cost overruns are common (Flyvbjerg: rail projects overrun about 45% on average, **verify**).
verification.finding: Prop1A bond authorization was2008, outside required example window. SB1029 Chapter152/2012 appropriated already-authorized bond proceeds; use it as an appropriation example, not new bond authorization. No ridership or construction-cost causal coefficient admitted.

verification.promptClaim: 3. **Short-line freight rail tax credit or grants.** State: Georgia, Oregon, Alabama and others (**verify** list). Federal: the 45G credit, made permanent in 2020. Effect: track upgraded to 286,000-pound cars keeps freight off roads and lowers road damage (**verify** size).
verification.finding: Oregon HB2164/2019 and Alabama HB457/2019 credit examples verified. Georgia HB588/2021 concerns freight grants/P3 authority, not proof of a short-line tax credit. Exhaustive state list, road-damage size remain unresearched; federal45G permanence is resolved in item2. Primary evidence adds MN2023/2025, MO2026 (eligible2027; agency implementation2028), WIAct242 signed2026, OK2020/2023 amendments and KS2022. Utah comparable maintenance credit remains unverified. This bounded seven-state set is not an exhaustive count.

verification.promptClaim: 3. **Short-line freight rail tax credit or grants.** State: Georgia, Oregon, Alabama and others (**verify** list). Federal: the 45G credit, made permanent in 2020. Effect: track upgraded to 286,000-pound cars keeps freight off roads and lowers road damage (**verify** size).
verification.finding: PL116-260 divisionEE§105 removed45G expiry in2020. Credit is40% for tax years starting2023 onward,50% before2023, capped at$3500 per eligible mile with assignment restrictions. Road-damage effect remains unsized.

verification.promptClaim: - **Federal:** the Safe Drinking Water Act sets enforceable maximum contaminant levels, a **federal floor**, and states run it with "primacy". verification.promptClaim: - **State:** broadband office, grant programs, **limits on municipal broadband**. About 16 states restrict public networks (BroadbandNow 2024, **verify**). North Carolina's HB 129 (2011) is an example.

verification.promptClaim: **Effects:** broadband availability raises employment and property values modestly (Kolko 2012; Whitacre and others 2014, **verify** sizes).
